questions.question: Explain the concept of food security and its four pillars.
questions.expected_answer: 1996 World Food Summit: all people, at all times, physical and economic access to sufficient, safe, nutritious food meeting dietary needs and preferences for active, healthy life. Availability (production, imports, storage, trade); access (income, prices, distance, grants); utilisation (varied diet, clean water, sanitation, fuel, safe preparation, health); stability (droughts, floods, prices, unemployment, conflict, pandemics). Food insecurity ranges from worry to hunger; stunting; obesity and diabetes from poor-quality diets.

questions.question: Describe food security and insecurity in the world and in South Africa, and their causes.
questions.expected_answer: World produces enough; about 700-800 million hungry (one in eleven), sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, conflict zones; waste in rich countries. SA nationally food secure (maize staple, exports citrus, grapes, wine) but about one in five households inadequate access; about 27% under-5 stunted (2016 SADHS); worst in rural Eastern Cape, KZN, Limpopo and informal settlements. Causes: unemployment, food prices, large share of income on food, apartheid land dispossession, drought and climate change, cost of nutritious food, disease. Responses: constitutional right to food, Child Support Grant, National School Nutrition Programme, food gardens, small farmers, COVID-19 SRD grant.

questions.question: Explain the role of science and technology in food production, including the Green Revolution, and evaluate its benefits and costs.
questions.expected_answer: Mechanisation, fertilisers (industrial nitrogen), pesticides/herbicides/fungicides, irrigation (Orange, Vaal, Olifants; over half SA water), breeding and hybrids. Green Revolution (1940s-70s, Borlaug): high-yield short-stemmed wheat and rice with fertiliser and irrigation; Mexico, India, Pakistan; India self-sufficient; Nobel 1970. Modern: biotechnology, precision agriculture, forecasting, apps, storage. Benefits: production outpaced population, more food per person, lower prices, less land cleared. Costs: eutrophication (Hartbeespoort), pesticide harm and resistance, waterlogging and salinisation, monoculture, fossil fuels and emissions; inequality, debt, fewer farm jobs, seed dependence, less success in Africa. Sustainable intensification: conservation agriculture, drip irrigation, integrated pest management, drought-tolerant varieties.
